genZNote: One of the smallest viruses that infects humans, but it packs a punch — 'slapped cheek' rash in kids, and a real danger to anyone with chronic hemolytic anemia or a developing fetus.

morphology.size: ~18-26 nm diameter (one of the smallest human viruses)

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human bone marrow erythroid progenitor cells and respiratory tract
habitat.hostAssociation: Humans are the sole natural host; specifically targets erythroid precursor cells via the P antigen receptor
habitat.reservoir: Infected humans, particularly school-age children during outbreaks

culture.growthCharacteristics: Does not grow in standard cell culture; diagnosis relies on serology (IgM/IgG) or PCR

identificationClues: One of the smallest and structurally simplest viruses known to infect humans
Classic 'slapped cheek' facial rash (erythema infectiosum, fifth disease) in children, often followed by a lacy reticular rash on the trunk/limbs
Directly infects and lyses erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow, which can precipitate transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolytic anemias (e.g., sickle cell disease)
Can cause fetal hydrops or fetal loss if a pregnant person is infected, due to severe fetal anemia — an important obstetric teaching point

diseases: Transient aplastic crisis (in chronic hemolytic anemia)
Chronic pure red cell aplasia (in immunocompromised patients)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Respiratory droplets, blood/blood products, and vertical (mother-to-fetus) transmission
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Common childhood infection with seasonal outbreaks, especially in schools; a well-recognized cause of complications in pregnancy and hemolytic anemia
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Serology (IgM for recent infection, IgG for past exposure) or PCR is used since it cannot be cultured by standard methods

examFacts.importantDisease: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum); aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemia; fetal hydrops
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: One of the smallest human viruses; directly attacks erythroid precursors, causing 'slapped cheek' rash and dangerous aplastic crises in susceptible hosts
